bibliography.abstract: Abstract Why do some informal neighborhoods receive public investment while others are neglected or evicted? This article addresses the inconsistent governmental responses to informal settlements in Jakarta, Indonesia, during the democratic period. State actions range from violent evictions to tolerance and community‐led improvements. These simultaneous operations of coercion, non‐intervention, and care suggest that the state's impulses in governing poverty are more heterogeneous than the literature predicts, which tends to attribute urban poor expulsions to capitalist expansion or colonial legacies. Urban poor movements have leveraged political contracts to push for pro‐poor policies, but implementation has remained uneven. Through a comparative analysis of five settlements in North Jakarta, based on field observations, interviews, and policy analysis, this research finds that the governance of informality depends on variations in community power, defined as the configuration of organizational capacity, external linkages, strategic capacity, and political embeddedness. Neighborhoods with stronger configurations across all dimensions were better able to access decision‐making arenas, align demands with elite priorities, and secure more accommodative treatment. This article reveals how discretionary authority from above intersects with power assembled from below to produce uneven outcomes within an already unequal field.

bibliography.title: EVICT, NEGLECT, OR INVEST? Community Power and the Politics of Urban Informality Governance in Jakarta

publication_status.journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research

en.caveats: The findings are based on a comparative analysis of five specific settlements within a single city, which may limit their direct applicability to different national or political contexts.
en.what: This study analyzes the governance of informal settlements in Jakarta through a comparative analysis of five neighborhoods in North Jakarta, utilizing field observations, interviews, and policy analysis. It examines why state responses to urban informality vary widely, ranging from violent evictions and neglect to collaborative, community-led infrastructure investments.
en.why: The research demonstrates that the treatment of informal settlements is not solely dictated by capitalist expansion or colonial legacies, but is actively shaped by community power. It establishes that neighborhoods with stronger organizational capacity, strategic alliances, and political embeddedness can successfully leverage discretionary state authority to secure accommodative policies.
